\section{Discussion}

A phaser is judged by its phased variants when its output is a phased VCF, but much of the use of long-read phasing is in the reads: a read left unphased is lost to every haplotype-resolved analysis, and a block of reads joined in the wrong orientation is worse. pgphase gains reads in two ways. It has more sites to phase them by: the graph's known alleles, read from where each read's alignment goes rather than called, and the sample's own heterozygous variants, so that fewer reads lack a site. And it is slow to join: the sites that make phasers misphase blocks of reads, collapsed duplications, poorly mapped stretches and homopolymer length calls, still label the reads that cross them but cannot hold two blocks together. The cost is more and shorter blocks than HiPhase's, where the reads cannot tell how blocks connect.

pgphase has limits. Its catalog holds only the alleles of the genomes in the graph: at a tandem repeat whose expansion in the sample no genome shares, a read's graph alignment takes the closest known walk, and the most of the switch errors we could not class are of this kind. It needs graph alignments of the reads, whose cost we do not count here, and more memory than the phasers it was compared with. We evaluated one sample and one technology; ONT reads, other samples and other graphs remain to be tested, and the development chromosomes shaped its rules even though the held-out ones were phased as well. Finally, a record-level comparison counts as switches differences of representation in repeats; classing switches by haplotype sequence, as here, or comparing haplotypes rather than records, would make phasers easier to compare.
